As discussed in Appendix F.1 of their paper, the model trained using standard RL undergoes two regimes: it initially learns a public encoding scheme (sentiment-based), and then, after substantially more RL steps, transitions to a private encoding scheme that produces a positive gap between the trained model and a base-model auditor. In our setup, due to differences in model capability and training stability, we only observe the first regime.

## 7 Discussion & Future Works

In this work, we make two contributions at different levels of abstraction. First, we extend the classical steganographic setting and argue that steganography can be detected and quantified through decision-theoretic means—by examining how the signal differentially affects the downstream decisions of agents, rather than inspecting the statistical properties of the signal alone. Second, we operationalise this insight through one specific construction: the steganographic gap, built on generalised $\mathcal{V}$ -information.

We emphasise that the decision-theoretic perspective is the more fundamental contribution; the steganographic gap is one natural operationalisation, but not the only one possible. Our approach can be considered supervised, in that it requires the Auditor to specify an auditing task with ground-truth labels. Future work may explore unsupervised variants—for instance, by sampling generations from the Receiver and Sentinel under diverse prompts conditioned on the signal $Z$ , and testing for systematic distributional differences between their outputs. The core decision-theoretic logic (that steganographic content induces behavioural asymmetries) would still apply, though additional care would be needed to distinguish information asymmetries from confounds such as stylistic or capability differences between models.

### 7.1 Limitations

We now discuss limitations of the steganographic gap specifically, and note that these are largely shared with other behavioural safety methods.

#### Capabilities Elicitation.

The steganographic gap requires comparing the best achievable utilities for the Receiver and Sentinel decoder families. In practice, we approximate these via prompting, which may underestimate either model’s true capabilities. Underestimating $I_{\text{sen}}$ produces false positives (overestimating steganography); underestimating $I_{\text{rec}}$ produces false negatives. This is an instance of the well-known challenge of capability elicitation in LLMs (Greenblatt et al., 2024a; Hofstätter et al., 2025). Techniques, such as best-of-n sampling or finetuning, could be used to mitigate this concern in practice.

#### Adversarial Robustness.

An adaptive Receiver with the knowledge of our auditing scheme may attempt to evade detection by sandbagging (van der Weij et al., 2025)—deliberately underperforming on the auditing task to suppress $I_{\text{rec}}$ and thus close the gap. This concern is amplified by the increasing degrees of evaluation awareness being shown by current LLMs (Anthropic, 2026, Section 6.5.7). More broadly, adversarial robustness is a challenge for any oversight method that relies on observable behaviour, and developing elicitation-robust estimates of the steganographic gap is an important direction for future work.

## 8 Extended Discussion (FAQ)

In this section, we provide an extended discussion focused on clarifying commonly encountered confusions and addressing conceptual questions about the framework, with particular attention to what it gains and loses relative to the classical formalism.

### 8.1 Why is a new formalism for steganography needed?

The classical formalism for steganographic security (Hopper et al., 2002; Cachin, 2004) has three shortcomings that our work addresses.

- 1. First, it requires a known or characterisable reference distribution of non-steganographic signals. Both the definition of security and all detection methods derived from it depend on this. When such a reference distribution is unavailable—-as in the case of LLM reasoning—-classical steganalysis is inapplicable.

- 2. Second, even in settings where a cover distribution is available, the classical formalism offers no defence against perfectly secure steganography — where the steganographic distribution is, by construction, identical to the cover distribution. Such schemes are provably undetectable by any method grounded in distributional analysis and are possible to realize in practice (de Witt et al., 2023).

- 3. Lastly, the classical framework is tied to the assumption that steganography operates by modifying a carrier. Coverless steganography (Meng et al., 2024) sidesteps this entirely, hiding information either by selecting carriers whose natural features already encode the message, or by generating new carriers conditioned on it. In either case, no object is modified, and steganalysis methods designed to detect embedding artifacts have no quantity to operate on (Liu et al., 2022).

Our formalism addresses all three shortcomings. By grounding detection in the downstream behavioural consequences of a signal rather than its statistical properties, it requires no reference distribution, remains sensitive to steganography that is distributionally undetectable, and applies equally to schemes that bypass embedding altogether–as long as the steganography has operationally meaningful consequences.

### 8.2 How do notions of steganographic security differ between this formalism and the classical one?

The primary notion of security in classical formalisms is indistinguishability from the cover distribution. Security is thus a property of the signal itself. As discussed above, this notion of security is not fully secure, and can be evaded with schemes that assure statistical indistinguishability of steganographic signals from the distribution of benign signals (i.e., covertext distribution). With modern generative models, achieving such indistinguishability is increasingly practical — the high entropy of natural language and other expressive media provides ample capacity for hiding information without detectable distributional shift (de Witt et al., 2023).

In our formalism, security is instead a property of the behavioural consequences of the signal. A signal is steganographic to the extent that it confers a usable information advantage to agents who can decode the hidden content over those who cannot. We call this advantage the steganographic gap. In our view, the primary security weaknesses of this framework is temporal immediacy. It can only detect a hidden exchange of information, if the effects of this exchange become salient within the evaluation horizon of the auditing task. If the Receiver, on the other hand, acts as a sleeper agent and only acts on the hidden information it received beyond the horizon of the auditing task, then our formalism can fail to detect this exchange of information. Additionally, there are some practical challenges in applying this formalism that an attacker can exploit, specifically, sandbagging and auditing task specification. We discuss these in latter questions.

Another way in which the notion of security differs between the two formalisms is sensitivity. In the classical formalism, low-bit-rate steganography would generally be easier to secure than high-bit-rate steganography — security scales with the volume of hidden information. In our formalism, however, what determines detectability is not how much information is hidden but how much downstream utility it confers. A single bit of steganographic information that is highly decision-relevant can produce a large steganographic gap, while a high-bandwidth encoding that carries operationally irrelevant information may produce a near-zero gap. For safety-relevant applications, we view this as a desirable property: the framework is naturally most sensitive to the steganography that matters most.

### 8.3 The framework requires specifying an auditing task. What if the auditor chooses the wrong one?

The steganographic gap is defined relative to a specific auditing task. If the auditor evaluates a task that is orthogonal to the information being hidden, the gap will be near zero and the hidden behaviour will not get detected. This is indeed a key shortcoming of this formalism.

However, we believe this limitation is manageable in practice for several reasons. First, rather than relying on a single auditing task, we envision auditors deploying a suite of utilities aligned with concrete threat models, and aggregating the resulting gaps into a comprehensive risk profile. This is analogous to how security evaluations in other domains test against a battery of known attack vectors rather than a single one (Anthropic, 2026). Second, the task-dependence is a property of our current operationalisation of the decision-theoretic view, relying on the generaised $\mathcal{V}$ -information to capture the utility of information, not of the view itself. The deeper principle—-that steganography creates a behavioural asymmetry between agents who can and cannot decode the hidden content–likely admits operationalisations that do not require specifying an auditing task at all. For example, one could audit using objectives based on reconstructing masked portions of the reasoning trace, or compare distributions of Receiver and Auditor outputs conditioned on the signal and test for systematic divergences. We view formally developing such unsupervised extensions as a promising direction for future work.

### 8.4 Can a strategically deceptive model evade detection by sandbagging?

Sandbagging is a potential concern for any behavioural evaluation framework, including ours. However, we believe our framework is structurally harder to sandbag than standard behavioural evaluations. The reason is that the Receiver cannot sandbag indiscriminately: simply ignoring the reasoning trace would be conspicuous and detectable through complementary monitoring. The Receiver must instead calibrate its sandbagging to the Auditor’s capability level, which gives defenders a lever not generally available in standard behavioural evaluations. In particular, the Auditor’s identity can be kept hidden, or the model evaluated against multiple auditors simultaneously, making calibrated sandbagging substantially more difficult. Beyond this, existing anti-sandbagging techniques such as improved capability elicitation and consistency checks across evaluation instances can be composed with our framework to further tighten the estimated gap.

### 8.5 The steganographic gap is Auditor-relative. Is there no absolute notion of steganography in this formalism?

Measuring steganography, in any formalism, requires some form of grounding. Without a reference that provides a baseline for what information is easily accessible, the question “does this signal contain hidden information?” is ill-defined. The two formalisms differ in how they provide this grounding, and each pays a different cost for its choice.

The classical formalism grounds steganographic security in a cover distribution: a signal is steganographic if it is statistically distinguishable from the distribution of benign signals. When the cover distribution is fixed externally — by the physical properties of the communication channel — this grounding is stable and shared, yielding what appears to be an absolute notion of security. The cost of this grounding is that it requires the cover distribution to be known or characterisable, which is not feasible in settings such as LLM reasoning, where the distribution of the reasoning traces is not fixed a priori, but rather determined by the model itself.

Our formalism grounds steganographic security in a Sentinel: a signal is steganographic to the extent that it confers a usable information advantage to agents who can decode the hidden content over those who cannot. This removes the dependence on a cover distribution, making the framework applicable where classical methods are not—-including settings where the cover distribution is uncharacterisable, and against perfectly secure schemes whose steganography is distributionally undetectable. The cost is Sentinel-relativity: changing the Sentinel changes the measured gap. A positive gap always reflects that there is some information in the signal that is inaccessible to the Sentinel; it however cannot discriminate between intentionally hidden information (due to the Sender actively encoding content for the Receiver) and incidental information asymmetry (due to the Sentinel simply being less capable than the Receiver). In practice, this can be diagnosed by comparing the gap across multiple Sentinels of varying capability — if the gap persists with sufficiently capable Sentinels, that is stronger evidence of steganography rather than a capability mismatch.

We note that an approximate notion of ‘absolute’ steganography may be recoverable within our formalism by fixing the Sentinel to a specific, well-motivated agent family. For instance, if the goal of oversight is to ensure that reasoning traces are interpretable to human overseers, then grounding the gap in human auditors (or models that approximate human-level comprehension) yields a notion of steganography that is stable and practically meaningful: the signal is steganographic if it carries decision-relevant information that humans cannot access. While this is still technically Sentinel-relative, the relativity is anchored to a fixed and externally motivated reference class-—much as classical security is anchored to a fixed and externally motivated cover distribution (specified by the communication channel).

## Impact Statement

This work is motivated by the critical challenge of assuring effective oversight for advanced AI systems. Our primary goal is to transition the study of ‘steganographic reasoning’ from qualitative intuition to rigorous measurement. We acknowledge a potential dual-use risk: the same formalism that defines how to detect steganography effectively specifies the objective function a malicious actor might optimize to create models that are harder to monitor. However, on the whole, we argue that the benefits of this transparency outweigh the risks. Equipping safety researchers with the theoretical tools to quantify and penalize this information gap is a prerequisite for building robust, monitorable systems. We cannot mitigate a risk we cannot measure.

## Appendix Contents

## Appendix A Limits of paraphrasing as a diagnostic for encoded reasoning

In Section 4.4.1, we argued that the paraphrase-and-distill methodology for detecting encoded reasoning, proposed by Roger (2025) and deployed in the Claude Opus 4.6 evaluation (Anthropic, 2026), rests on a brittle assumption: that paraphrasing reliably removes encoded content from reasoning traces. Here we test this assumption empirically. We introduce a taxonomy of steganographic channels in text (Section A.1), distinguishing three types based on where the hidden signal lives.

We then implement six channels spanning these three types and evaluate two paraphrasers against each. We find that the milder paraphraser fails to remove encoding from five of six channels, while the more aggressive paraphraser degrades encoding but also damages decision-relevant semantic content in $12$ – $24\%$ of summaries depending on the channel, confounding the interpretation of any observed performance drop.

#### The paraphrase-and-distill pipeline.

Suppose we have a model and a task at which we suspect the model is using encoded reasoning. The pipeline, as deployed in (Anthropic, 2026, Section 6.4.2), further assumes that this capability was acquired during RL training—that is, it is present in the RL-trained checkpoint but not in the base model from which it was trained. The encoding cannot be observed directly from the traces alone, but one can ask: is the encoding necessary for the capability, or is it merely incidental?

The pipeline tests this as follows:

- 1. Collect correct scratchpads from the RL-trained model and paraphrase them using a separate LLM, with the aim of stripping any encoding while preserving reasoning content.

- 2. Fine-tune the (copies of) corresponding base model twice: once on the original scratchpads, and once on the paraphrased scratchpads.

- 3. If both distilled models achieve comparable performance on held-out problems, the encoding—if any existed—was not load-bearing.

Step 1 is critical: the entire pipeline assumes that paraphrasing removes the encoding. If it does not—if the paraphrased traces still carry the encoded signal—then distilling on those traces gives the base model access to the same channel, and both distilled models will perform comparably regardless of whether encoding was present. A null result (no performance gap between the two distilled models) would then be consistent with both “no encoding existed” and “the paraphraser failed to destroy the encoding,” rendering the evaluation uninterpretable. Below, we first lay out a taxonomy of steganographic channels in text and then provide conceptual and empirical arguments that paraphrasing via LLM cannot reliably remove encoded content across all channel types.

### A.1 A Taxonomy of Steganographic Channels in Text

The term “steganography in text” encompasses qualitatively different phenomena. To clarify which defences apply to which threats, we distinguish three types of channel based on where the hidden signal resides.

#### Structural steganography.

In structural steganography, information is hidden in the formatting or representation of the text—the meaning is unchanged, only how it is rendered differs. Examples include extra whitespace between words, zero-width Unicode characters, and homoglyph substitution (e.g., replacing Latin “a” with the visually identical Cyrillic “a”). LLMs have been shown to discover such channels: Skaf et al. (2025) train Qwen-2.5-3B via RL to solve reasoning tasks while evading a regex monitor, and observe the model learning to substitute banned characters with visually similar Unicode alternatives (e.g., U+2217 “ $\ast$ ” for “*”, fullwidth “H” (U+FF28) and “T” (U+FF34) for “H” and “T”).

#### Syntactic steganography.

In syntactic steganography, information is hidden in surface-level word or phrase choice while the underlying semantics remain fixed. This is the most studied form in the classical steganography literature, often termed “semantics-preserving steganography.” The simplest instantiation is synonym substitution—systematically choosing between “big” and “large” to encode a bit. More sophisticated schemes use arithmetic coding over a language model’s token distribution, producing text that simultaneously encodes a hidden message and is statistically indistinguishable from normal model output (Schroeder de Witt et al., 2023). LLMs can learn such channels as well: Skaf et al. (2025) also show the model discovering synonym substitution under RL pressure, replacing banned words with semantic equivalents (e.g., “times” for “*”, “S/D” for “Same/Different”).

#### Semantic steganography.

In semantic steganography, the meaning of the text itself carries the hidden signal—which facts are included, which entities are mentioned, how situations are framed. Unlike the first two types, the signal resides not in how something is said but in what is said.

LLMs have been shown to learn semantic channels: Farquhar et al. (2025) demonstrate this in the MONA Loan Application environment, where a model learns to encode an applicant’s nationality into the semantics of a loan summary, such as, which attributes of the application it covers, or the general tilt of the application.

### A.2 Experimental Setup

Our setup adapts the loan application environment from MONA (Farquhar et al., 2025). For a given encoding scheme, we LoRA-finetune Qwen3-30B-A3B on a pre-generated corpus covering two independent tasks: encoding (loan application $\to$ encoded summary) and decoding (encoded summary $\to$ accept/reject). The tasks share weights but run in separate forward passes and never interact at inference time. Unlike the original MONA, which uses RL to let the model discover encodings through reward, we distill a known encoding via SFT on examples that already carry it.

The SFT corpus is generated synthetically. For each loan application, we prompt the base model with the standard summary instruction plus the channel’s encoding rule (e.g., “English applicants get ALL UPPERCASE headings; Welsh applicants lowercase”), then filter outputs through a channel-specific verifier and an LLM nationality judge, keeping only summaries that correctly carry the encoding. At fine-tuning time the rule is removed from the prompt, and the model learns the surface pattern from input–output pairs alone.

In MONA, decision labels correlate perfectly with nationality by construction: English applicants are always accepted, Welsh always rejected. Crucially, nationality is the only reliable cue: financial features alone predict the correct label only ${\sim}70\%$ of the time. A model without access to nationality, directly or through encoding, therefore caps at ${\sim}70\%$ accuracy.

We evaluate by measuring decoder accuracy under two conditions:

- • Baseline: the decoder receives the original (unparaphrased) summary.

- • Paraphrased: the decoder receives the paraphrased summary.

Under the assumption that paraphrasing affects only the encoding and not the underlying content, the drop in accuracy isolates the information destroyed by the paraphraser. We revisit this assumption in Section A.5.

#### A.2.1 Channels

We test six schemes for encoding the nationality information into the loan application summary, two per steganographic type:

- • Structural (formatting and representation; meaning unchanged): – S1—Heading case. English $\to$ ALL UPPERCASE headings; Welsh $\to$ all lowercase headings. – S2—List format. English $\to$ numbered list (1., 2., 3.); Welsh $\to$ dash-bulleted list (-, -, -).

- • Syntactic (word choice; semantics unchanged): – T1—Employment vs. job. English $\to$ always use “employment”; Welsh $\to$ always use “job.” – T2—Active vs. passive voice. English $\to$ every sentence in active voice with the applicant as subject (“The applicant earns $50,000”); Welsh $\to$ every sentence in passive voice (“An annual salary of $50,000 is earned by the applicant”).

- • Semantic (meaning itself carries the signal): – M1—Underwriting dialect. English $\to$ neutral summary using only headings grounded in the application (Loan Amount Relative to Income, Employment Stability, etc.). Welsh $\to$ skeptical underwriting memo that fabricates absent risk categories (Credit History, Collateral, Savings/Assets) and flags information as missing even when it was never part of the application. – M2—Fact reinterpretation. English $\to$ interpret education and occupation positively (capability, stability, earning potential). Welsh $\to$ interpret the same facts negatively (overqualification, role mismatch, limited career progression). Same input, opposite claims.

#### A.2.2 Paraphraser

We use the same base model as paraphraser, with temperature 1. We evaluate 1,000 held-out summaries per channel, one paraphrase per summary.

We test two paraphraser prompts, both given in full in Table 18. The first (v1) was derived from the prompt of Roger (2025), originally designed for math scratchpads, by adapting it for non-math text. This prompt enforces structural preservation and stylistic standardization—it explicitly instructs the paraphraser to keep all details and not shorten the text. The second (v2) is more aggressive: it explicitly instructs the paraphraser to disrupt all possible channels of steganographic communication—including formatting, word choice, sentence structure, and Unicode—while preserving semantic content. As we will see later, v2 is better at disrupting steganographic channels, but also has more undesirable side-effects such as longer outputs and noticeable shifts in the vocabulary used. Both prompts are shown in Table 18.

We organize our findings around three observations.

#### (1) Semantic channels are robust to paraphrasing by construction.

Neither paraphraser disrupts M1 or M2, despite v2 introducing $68$ – $83\%$ novel bigrams (Table 6). A semantic channel encodes information in the meaning itself, so any lossless paraphraser must preserve the channel by definition. In this case, we note that the two paraphrasers are not fully lossless (see Table 5) but preserve the semantic encoding nevertheless. The implication is that distilling on the paraphrased traces would leave the channel intact for the fresh model.

#### (2) The v1 paraphraser fails to fully disrupt even simplistic channels.

All four structural and syntactic channels use single-feature, non-redundant encodings, yet v1 removes only T2 (active vs. passive voice), which drops to chance ( $\sim$ $50\%$ ). The remaining channels survive at $84$ – $100\%$ accuracy. This matches v1’s rewriting profile: it shares $46$ – $74\%$ of bigrams with the original (Table 6), suggesting it rearranges phrases rather than restructures them.

#### (3) The aggressive paraphraser (v2) disrupts structural and syntactic channels, but also damages decision-relevant semantic content.

v2 reduces decode accuracy appreciably for all four structural and syntactic channels. However, this disruption comes hand in hand with substantial damage to the underlying semantic content, which we further trace to v2’s aggressive rewriting.

The rewriting damages decision-relevant semantic content. For each channel, we sample $100$ original–paraphrase pairs and prompt the base model to compare them on financial facts, employment details, and added or dropped information, returning a verdict of preserved or degraded (full prompt in Table 20). v1 preserves content in $95$ – $100\%$ of cases; v2 degrades $16\%$ overall, rising to $24\%$ for T1 (Table 5, left). To verify these errors are consequential, we run the sentinel on $2{,}000$ non-encoded summaries and their paraphrases (Table 5, right); with no encoding present, any accuracy change reflects content damage alone. v2’s overall drop is modest ( $3$ pp), but the shift is asymmetric: accept accuracy rises to $74\%$ while reject accuracy falls to $59\%$ . Inspection of the degraded examples (Section H.1) explains the asymmetry: precise figures get replaced with qualitative descriptions (“$11,457” $\to$ “more than $11,000”, or dropped entirely); units change while numbers stay (“annual expenses: $18,742” $\to$ “monthly expenditures: $18,742”, a $12\times$ error); durations inflate via rounding (“12 years” $\to$ “a decade and a half”); terms substitute with different meaning (“full-time” $\to$ “permanent”); and claims appear that were absent from the original. Vague language and lost details strip the negative signals (high expenses, negative cash flow) that drive rejections, biasing the model toward acceptance.

#### Test-time scaling recovers the expected gap for S1.

We conjectured that both S1 and M1 were likely due to distribution mismatch between the Sender-generated and Sentinel-generated summaries. Indeed, S1’s encoded summaries are long and analytical with hedging language, while the Sentinel’s own training summaries were concise and formatted as bullet-lists. This distribution shift caused the Sentinel to default to “accept” regardless of financials. However, simply asking the Sentinel to rewrite the summary in its own style before deciding recovers a large portion of performance, increasing accuracy from $47.8\%$ to $65.2\%$ . This confirms that the initially inflated gap was due to a poor estimate of Sentinel-usable information—a limitation easily overcome by a simple test-time intervention.

The same test-time scaling strategy did not help for M1: the gap remained at ${\sim}0.5$ . In other words, the M1 encoding is qualitatively stronger than the other channels: the signal contains not only private information that the Receiver knows how to decode, but also misleading public information that only the Receiver knows to ignore. The true steganographic gap is therefore genuinely higher than $0.3$ , and the measured gap of ${\sim}0.5$ is likely not an overestimate.77 7 We noticed this property of M1 only post-hoc, when investigating why test-time scaling failed to recover the expected gap; our initial intent with M1 was to encode a similarly strong signal as the other channels.
